legend: Petya has an array of integers a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ0%%. He only likes sorted arrays. Unfortunately, the given array could be arbitrary, so Petya wants to sort it.

Petya likes to challenge himself, so he wants to sort array using only 3%%ZSMJ1%%-cycles. More formally, in one operation he can pick 3%%ZSMJ2%% pairwise distinct indices i%%ZSMJ3%%, j%%ZSMJ4%%, and k%%ZSMJ5%% (1≤i,j,k≤n%%ZSMJ6%%) and apply i→j→k→i%%ZSMJ7%% cycle to the array a%%ZSMJ8%%. It simultaneously places ai%%ZSMJ9%% on position j%%ZSMJ10%%, aj%%ZSMJ11%% on position k%%ZSMJ12%%, and ak%%ZSMJ13%% on position i%%ZSMJ14%%, without changing any other element.
For example, if a%%ZSMJ15%% is [10,50,20,30,40,60]%%ZSMJ16%% and he chooses i=2%%ZSMJ17%%, j=1%%ZSMJ18%%, k=5%%ZSMJ19%%, then the array becomes [50_,40_,20,30,10_,60]%%ZSMJ20%%.
Petya can apply arbitrary number of 3%%ZSMJ21%%-cycles (possibly, zero). You are to determine if Petya can sort his array a%%ZSMJ22%%, i. e. make it non-decreasing.
input: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases t%%ZSMJ23%% (1≤t≤5⋅105%%ZSMJ24%%). Description of the test cases follows.
The first line of each test case contains a single integer n%%ZSMJ25%% (1≤n≤5⋅105%%ZSMJ26%%) — the length of the array a%%ZSMJ27%%.
The second line of each test case contains n%%ZSMJ28%% integers a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ29%% (1≤ai≤n%%ZSMJ30%%).
It is guaranteed that the sum of n%%ZSMJ31%% over all test cases does not exceed 5⋅105%%ZSMJ32%%.
output: For each test case, print "YES" (without quotes) if Petya can sort the array a%%ZSMJ33%% using 3%%ZSMJ34%%-cycles, and "NO" (without quotes) otherwise. You can print each letter in any case (upper or lower).
note: In the 6%%ZSMJ35%%-th test case Petya can use the 3%%ZSMJ36%%-cycle 1→3→2→1%%ZSMJ37%% to sort the array.
In the 7%%ZSMJ38%%-th test case Petya can apply 1→3→2→1%%ZSMJ39%% and make a=[1,4,2,3]%%ZSMJ40%%. Then he can apply 2→4→3→2%%ZSMJ41%% and finally sort the array.
